title: Changeup wear-out per earlier look
note: Each earlier changeup or splitter a hitter saw from this pitcher in earlier plate appearances today, in place of another pitch type, goes with 1.87 fewer whiff points per swing on the next one (base rate 31.9%). Observational: an association with fixed effects and controls, not a randomized test.

title: After four or more changeups today
note: Whiff% per swing on changeups and splitters for a hitter who has seen 4+ of them from this pitcher earlier today, against one who has seen none, holding total pitches seen fixed. That is a quarter of the pitch's whiff rate, and the cost keeps climbing with each look.

chip: 42% carries to the next same-handed pitcher
title: Wear-out carries to the next pitcher
note: Each changeup a hitter saw from a same-handed pitcher earlier today goes with 0.79 fewer whiff points on the next pitcher's changeup, about two fifths of the same-pitcher effect. The other-hand carryover is smaller and not significant, so hand is a lean, not a rule.

title: Exposure index fails out of sample
note: If the hitter-exposure index meant what it says, a plate appearance's run value would rise one-for-one with it. On 2026, a season the costs never saw, slope 1 is rejected (p < 0.001): the per-pitch cost holds but doesn't reach plate-appearance runs.

title: Managers don't pull on exposure
rows: Run value allowed so far, per SD
note: Change in the chance a manager removes the starter before the next PA, per run/100 PAs of the next hitter's exposure index, in 2026. No detectable response; pricing the index the way managers price times through is ruled out.

title: The planned test on held-out 2026
note: Whiff points per swing per SD of similar-shape exposure from other pitchers in the last 30 days. It passed the plan's rule on the held-out season, but its placebo failed, so the plan reports it as confounded.

title: The placebo that sank the test
note: Shapes a hitter is about to see in the next 30 days can't cause today's whiffs, yet they predict them. Something stable links hitters to the shapes they face; the likeliest reason is selection over who plays against what.

title: Small recent effect, season held fixed
rows: about 2 runs (0.5 to 3.8), an upper bound
note: Recent exposure still matters a little once his whole-season diet of that shape is held fixed, and this version passes its placebo. Exploratory: no held-out season, and no single season clears zero alone.

title: Bat speed reads in one game
note: Bat speed is half signal after about 3 competitive swings, faster than anything else measured on a hitter, and it carries into next season. Because it reads so fast, regressing it changes almost nothing beyond a few games.

title: wOBA needs most of a season
note: wOBA's fitted reliability curve doesn't reach r = 0.5 until about 500 PA, beyond the largest sample the data allow, so it is an extrapolation. Full-time hitters are more alike and need more.

title: Regressing beats raw numbers
note: Regressing toward the league mean beat the raw number out of sample for 135 of the 147 metric groups that could be scored. 2026 was also the development test set, so the clean replication is the stronger check.

title: Four-seam ride, the best lever
rows: Whiff pts per 2 in more ride
note: Each 2 inches of added four-seam ride from one season to the next goes with 1.62 more whiff points per swing, net of the league and prior-season results. Observational, and the year-two interval is wide.

title: Velocity gains may be recovery
note: Next year's velocity gain 'predicts' last year's whiff drop, which it can't have caused, so recovery from a down year isn't ruled out. Read it as: pitchers whose velocity comes back get their whiffs back.

title: The sample behind the levers
note: Each pair is the same pitcher and pitch type in consecutive seasons, both above the pitch and swing floors. Pitchers chose these changes, so every result is an association with controls, matching and a placebo.

title: Tax engine checked against real bills
rows: 2025 luxury-tax bills, each club that paid
42.5% vs 45% surcharge goes by payor status
note: The CBT engine was run on each club's published 2025 payroll and reproduced the published bill to the dollar or within rounding. The Red Sox gap is reported, not adjusted; no source explains it.

title: Skenes extension: open and walk-away
note: Present value at a 10% discount, priced under both the current rules and MLB's proposed 16% own-club maximum. The injury and rule-change chances are illustrative assumptions, not estimates.

title: Division rivals trade far less
rows: Poisson, all 435 pairs, club volume fixed
note: Rival pairs complete a little over half as many trades as comparable non-rival pairs. It counts completed trades only, not offers, and doesn't say why rivals avoid each other.

title: How broad the rival gap is
note: Expected counts come from each club's trade volume alone. No single pair is significant after a false-discovery correction across 435 pairs; the finding is the pooled one.

title: Every MLB trade since 2009
rows: Two-club trades in the pair model
note: Every trade is loaded into a Neo4j graph with the WAR each club got. The feed records fewer trades in 2009–11 and appears to miss many minor-league-only deals early on.

title: Front-office ties and trade rate
note: A pair of clubs trades about 18% more in seasons when its decision-makers share front-office history than in its own other seasons. It is observational; a hire that coincides with a rebuild could also move the rate.

title: Permutation check on any tie
rows: rotate each pair's tied seasons, refit
note: Shuffling when each pair was tied almost never produces an effect this large, so the any-tie result isn't an artifact of the standard errors. The test doesn't rely on the cluster standard errors that can run small with these fixed effects.

title: Protégé facing his old boss
note: The narrow tie behind the Angels–Braves story leans positive but isn't confirmed. It depends on that one pair, and the permutation p is about twice the cluster-based one.

title: Where future heads worked first
rows: 15 future heads, 9 in a top job today
note: Counts people who worked in a club's front office before their first head job. Big departments and long tenures put more people on record, and the study can't say how much starting in Cleveland raises anyone's odds.

title: The path to the chair
note: Measured from the first recorded front-office job. Former major-league players move fastest, and hire dates follow the career records, which can move a path by one year.

title: Overall future grade and role
rows: B1: closer or high-leverage reliever, now and in 2027
note: OFP is the scout's single summary grade on the 20-80 scale, rolled up from the pitch grades; graded as a reliever because he throws almost no changeups to lefties and his longest 2026 outing was 40 pitches. Risk is moderate: the velocity gain and the changeup's share are recent, and there is an elbow history.

title: How often hitters miss his changeup
note: A low-spin, splitter-like tumbler that drops 10.4 in more than his sinker. The biggest question is how much of the miss rate survives a second year of hitters seeing it at 92 mph.

title: What needs eyes, not data
rows: tempo, time to the plate, effort, landing, arm action, fielding
note: There has been no live or video look, so the delivery items a scout grades by eye are left as NG (no grade). Tracking data covers slot and release consistency, which is not the same as command; the report asks for a video look before any bid.

title: Skubal's changeup miss rate, two seasons
note: Pooling two seasons gives the stable read: even the low end of the interval is far above the league norm. The league whiff norms are approximate, not matched to 2025.

title: How rarely the Rays swing and miss
note: The nine regulars put the ball in play and do little with it, so outs have to come from weak contact more than strikeouts. Rates use 2026 regular-season pitches only and treat every pitch they saw as league-average.

chip: coach page in English and Spanish
title: The one-page plan for pitchers
rows: the nine regulars plus four off the bench
Caminero lets 3 of every 4 first pitches go
Dylan's translation, to be reviewed by a Spanish-speaking coach
note: The full packet boiled down to plain plan lines a staff can use in the dugout; every number behind a line is in the full packet. The Spanish page is a translation still under review.

title: How well the comp line fits
rows: about 1.4% per platform save, 0.7% per career save
Edwin Díaz and Megill, each about 32%
note: Leave-one-out refits the line without each closer and checks how far off it is for him, so 16% is the honest error for a new case like Smith's. ERA, strikeouts and All-Star selection added nothing clearly different from zero.

title: Club's odds at a hearing
rows: If the panel reads the comps
If the panel reads the market
note: The panel picks the figure nearer its own value, so the base case averages two views of that value with even weight. The club stays the favorite until the panel puts about 73% of its weight on the market view.

title: Do swing decisions repeat?
note: Decision value is a stable skill, steadier year to year than wOBA. But it adds nothing to next season's wOBA forecast once wOBA and xwOBA are known: it says which part of a line will hold.

title: Torres's 2027 projection and value
rows: two years, $28-32M; walk away above $17M a year
note: Two-year value is in present value, with a 3% yearly raise in the price of a win, a 10% discount rate and an aging path. The big unknown is whether the bat speed he lost in 2026 comes back.
